90: Grain shape ranks among the most strongly inherited of all quality traits, being fixed by the maternal genotype during grain filling, so that the varietal differences recorded here are to be expected. All three landraces fall well short of the slender Basmati grain type described by Kaul (1970), which confirms their membership of the small and medium grained group of Indian aromatic rices catalogued by Singh et al. (2000). Pachauri et al. (2010) observed that short, round aromatic landraces may equal or surpass Basmati in flavour and digestibility even where grain shape counts against them in the market, an observation applicable to the present material. The slight contraction registered during storage most probably reflects uneven shrinkage rather than any genuine change in shape: as bound moisture leaves the kernel it contracts more along its length than across its breadth, so that the ratio declines marginally. Since the change is very small it carries no commercial consequence, and it registers as significant only because the experimental error in this trial was low.

110: The moisture content of stored paddy is not a fixed property of the lot but a running equilibrium with the surrounding air. Genkawa et al. (2008) demonstrated that brown rice held under ambient conditions continues to exchange water vapour with the atmosphere, so that this equilibrium, rather than the initial moisture content of the grain, is what governs storability. The rise and fall recorded across the sampling dates therefore tracks the seasonal humidity of the Gangetic plain, the grain drying through the cool months and reabsorbing moisture during the monsoon. The varietal differences are most probably a matter of husk structure, since a tight, closely fitting husk retards vapour movement and maintains the kernel in a damper state than a loose one. This carries practical weight, since the same godown will not afford every landrace the same margin of safety. Nearly all samples remained within the limit prescribed for safe paddy storage (IRRI, 2016), and Müller et al. (2022) recommend holding grain within a comparable band. Duangkhamchan et al. (2024) further demonstrated that moisture is seldom uniformly distributed through a stored heap, so that portions of a lot may exceed the safe limit even where the mean appears acceptable.

132: The progressive loss of aroma through storage constitutes the most consequential finding of this experiment, and its cause is well established. The fragrance of aromatic rice derives chiefly from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, a highly volatile compound detectable at very low concentration (Buttery et al., 1983; Bhattacharjee et al., 2002). Yoshihashi et al. (2002) demonstrated that the plant synthesises this compound while the grain is still filling and synthesises no further quantity after harvest, so that any loss in store is irreversible. Simple volatilisation, assisted by slow oxidation, is therefore the most probable basis of the decline. Widjaja et al. (1996) traced the same reduction in the volatile fraction of paddy, brown and white fragrant rice, and Wongpornchai et al. (2004) recorded it in a fragrant cultivar with increasing storage time. Yoshihashi et al. (2005) demonstrated the rate to be governed principally by storage temperature, which accounts for the severity of the loss under ambient conditions in eastern India. The pronounced varietal ranking reflects genetic control of the biosynthetic pathway, while the smaller effect of growing site is most probably attributable to differences in the supply of precursor amino acids during grain filling, as Itani et al. (2004) proposed and Imran et al. (2023) subsequently confirmed. Kim et al. (2023) add the caution that sensory quality may decline well before any outward indication of deterioration becomes apparent.
